Lessons.Title: Rewriting Quadratic Expressions in Factored Form (Part 2)
ExplanationParagraphs: Learning goal: factor monic trinomials whose two constant factors have opposite signs, reason about positive versus negative products, and verify linear coefficients through sum/product. Independently authored Edulytiks adaptation of Illustrative Mathematics Algebra 1 First Edition Unit 7 Lesson 7 teacher https://im.kendallhunt.com/HS/teachers/1/7/7/preparation.html and student https://im.kendallhunt.com/HS/students/1/7/7/index.html (CC BY 4.0). The source extends earlier two-sum/two-difference factors to one sum and one difference.

Original expression x²−x−12. Need integers m,n whose product−12 and sum−1. The pair−4 and+3 works: (x−4)(x+3)=x²−x−12. The mixed-sign factors explain why constant is negative but x coefficient may be positive or negative depending on magnitude.

Another first-party trinomial x²+2x−15 uses product−15 and sum+2, from+5 and−3, so (x+5)(x−3). Expand to verify all terms; at x0 constant is−15, and at x3 the product vanishes. Do not treat a negative constant as proof that the larger-in-magnitude factor must be negative; check coefficient sign.

Student task: list integer factor pairs of a negative number, choose by required sum, build a signed-area reasoning table, factor both expressions and critique the tempting pair+4,−3 for x²−x−12. Teacher-scored rubric0–2 for signed factor search, identity algebra, verification and explanation.

KeyConcepts.Title: Opposite signs
KeyConcepts.Definition: If integer factor product is negative, the two constant factors have opposite signs.

KeyConcepts.Title: Linear coefficient
KeyConcepts.Definition: The sum m+n sets the coefficient of x in monic expansion.
KeyConcepts.Rule: Check signed sum, not just magnitudes.

KeyConcepts.Title: Identity check
KeyConcepts.Definition: Expand all factor products to confirm entire polynomial.

WorkedExamples.Title: Factor negative linear coefficient
WorkedExamples.Question: Factor x²−x−12.
WorkedExamples.Method: Show distributive or equivalence-preserving algebra and independently verify every candidate solution.

WorkedExamples.Title: Factor positive linear coefficient
WorkedExamples.Question: Factor x²+2x−15.
WorkedExamples.Method: Show distributive or equivalence-preserving algebra and independently verify every candidate solution.

WorkedExamples.Title: Reject reversed signs
WorkedExamples.Question: Would (x+4)(x−3) equal x²−x−12?
WorkedExamples.Method: Show distributive or equivalence-preserving algebra and independently verify every candidate solution.
Steps: So it matches a different polynomial.
WorkedExamples.Answer: No; the middle coefficient has wrong sign.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Changing both signs when only one should be negative
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: Two negative factors have positive product.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Use opposite signs for negative constant.

SummaryPoints: Mixed signs correspond to negative constant products.
Use the signed sum to select the correct factor order.
